newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro rights court to hear Britons' N-test charges.
newsitem.headline: Euro rights court to hear Britons' N-test charges.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights will hear charges by three Britons over exposure to nuclear weapons tests in the South Pacific in the 1950s, the court said on Thursday.

In one case, two British soldiers allege they suffered health problems from radiation in the tests and that London then violated their human rights by denying them access to medical records from the time.

In the other case referred to the court, a 30-year-old woman says that she suffered leukaemia because the British government had failed to inform her father, also exposed to the nuclear tests, of the risks of radiation.
In a statement, the court set no date for hearings.
Between 1962 and 1967 Britain carried out nuclear tests above ground in Australia and Christmas Island. More than 20,000 servicemen took part.

The first two applicants, Kenneth McGinley and a man named only as Mr E, were among many who had to line up in light clothing to monitor the effects of a blast several miles (km) away, the court said.

In failed appeals to the Pensions Tribunal, the two "have been unable to gain access to contemporaneous records containing detailed information on the tests and relating to medical evidence in support of their claims," it said.

The European Commission of Human Rights, which vets cases for the court, reckoned in an opinion in November that Britain had deprived them of a fair hearing before the Pensions Tribunal and that this constituted a failure to respect their private lives, it said.

But the Commission reckoned there was no evidence of a breach of the European Convention of Human Rights in the woman's case, saying there was no evidence that an earlier diagnosis would have let doctors pre-empt the development of her disease.
